title: Time Series and Trend Analysis
summary: A time series is data recorded in order of time. This chapter explains its four components and two methods of measuring the secular trend: moving averages and the method of least squares, which is also used for forecasting.

notes.heading: Time series and its uses
notes.html:
A time series is a set of observations of a variable arranged chronologically, usually at equal intervals: yearly sales, monthly rainfall, daily share prices.

  • Time is the independent variable (t); the observed value is the dependent variable (Y).
  • Uses: understanding past behaviour, forecasting, planning and budgeting, comparing actual performance with expected performance.
  • Univariate time series: a single variable recorded over time.

notes.heading: Components of a time series
notes.html:
ComponentNatureExample
Secular trend (T)Long-term smooth upward or downward movementRising population, falling death rate
Seasonal variation (S)Regular pattern repeating within a yearWoollen sales in winter, festival demand
Cyclical variation (C)Ups and downs lasting more than a year (business cycle: boom, recession, depression, recovery)Trade cycles
Irregular variation (I)Random, unpredictable, short-livedFloods, strikes, a pandemic

Models: Additive Y = T + S + C + I; Multiplicative Y = T × S × C × I.

notes.heading: Moving average method
notes.html:
A moving average of period k is the mean of k consecutive values, written against the middle of the period. It smooths out short-term fluctuations to reveal the trend.

  • For an even period (e.g. 4-yearly) the average falls between two years, so we centre it: take the mean of two successive moving averages.
  • Limitation: no trend values for the first and last few years, and it cannot be used directly for forecasting.

notes.heading: Method of least squares: odd number of years
notes.html:
Fit the straight line Y = a + bx, where x = year − middle year, so that Σx = 0. Then a = ΣY/n and b = ΣxY/Σx2.

notes.heading: Method of least squares: even number of years
notes.html:
The origin is taken midway between the two middle years and x is measured in half-year units: x = (year − mid-point)/0.5, giving …, −5, −3, −1, 1, 3, 5, …

Example 3

Years 2018–2023, Y: 10, 13, 15, 18, 20, 26. Origin = 2020.5; x: −5, −3, −1, 1, 3, 5.

ΣY = 102, so a = 102/6 = 17. ΣxY = −50 − 39 − 15 + 18 + 60 + 130 = 104. Σx2 = 25 + 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 + 25 = 70. b = 104/70 = 1.486.

Trend: Y = 17 + 1.486x. For 2024, x = 7: Y = 17 + 10.4 = 27.4.

notes.heading: Common mistakes
notes.html:
• Writing a moving average against the wrong year; it belongs to the middle of its period.
  • Forgetting to centre moving averages of even period.
  • Using unit steps (−2.5, −1.5, …) and then mixing them with half-year steps for an even number of years. Stick to one scale.
  • Not stating the origin and unit of x with the trend equation.
  • Calling a festival-season rise 'cyclical': anything repeating within a year is seasonal.

keyTerms.definition: Data arranged in chronological order at regular intervals.

Oscillations with a period longer than a year, linked to business cycles.

questions.q: Name the four components of a time series.
questions.answerHtml: Secular trend, seasonal variation, cyclical variation and irregular variation.

questions.q: Distinguish between seasonal and cyclical variations.
questions.answerHtml: Seasonal variations repeat regularly within one year and are caused by climate and custom (e.g. umbrella sales in monsoon). Cyclical variations have a period of more than a year, are not of fixed length and are caused by business cycles (boom, recession, depression, recovery).
